Memory.value: Something in my surroundings can instantly bring back the full memory without warning
My memories of the frightening event are very clear and detailed.
Remembering the event brings back the same terror I felt at the time

Negative Appraisals.value: The people or institutions that should have protected me let me down
I feel like I don't know myself anymore
I have permanently changed for the worse

vignette:
Margaret stood at the front desk of the midtown hotel she had managed for fifteen years, her hands gripping the polished mahogany edge as a group of young men in dark jackets pushed through the revolving doors. The sight hit her without warning—a cold rush that seized her chest before her mind could catch up. She was not in the lobby anymore. She was back on the sidewalk outside her own apartment building, four years ago, watching the patrol car screech to a halt. Her husband Thomas had been reaching for his wallet to show his ID, the same gesture he had made a thousand times, and the officer had seen only a threat. The memory was so clear she could still count the buttons on the officer’s uniform, still feel the concrete bite into her knees as she was forced to the ground. The terror that flooded her now was the same terror that had torn through her then—undiminished, as though the four years between had never happened.

The anniversary of that night came every March, and Margaret had learned to dread the weeks leading up to it with a quiet, grinding certainty. She had stopped marking the date on her calendar, but her body remembered. Her sleep would fray, her appetite would vanish, and unwanted thoughts would press into her mind at the worst moments—while she was approving a banquet order, while a guest asked a simple question at check-in. The thoughts came without invitation, carrying fragments of the sound of Thomas’s breath catching, the sight of his glasses skidding across the pavement, the weight of the officer’s boot on her back. She had come to believe that the institutions that were supposed to protect them—the police, the city, the very system she had trusted her whole life—had failed not just in that moment but fundamentally, irreparably. She had been a woman who believed in order, in rules, in the basic decency of authority. That woman was gone. She felt like a stranger to herself now, someone brittle and watchful, someone who saw menace in the ordinary shape of a uniformed security guard or the sudden approach of a stranger on the street.

Crowded places had become impossible. The hotel’s annual gala, once her favorite event, now sent her heart racing before she even entered the ballroom. She had begun delegating the evening shift to her assistant manager, inventing reasons about paperwork and back-office tasks. The avoidance had spread quietly, like a stain seeping through fabric. She stopped taking the subway. She stopped attending the neighborhood association meetings she had chaired for a decade. She told herself she was just tired, just getting older, but she knew the truth: she was afraid. The world felt permanently dangerous, and she felt permanently damaged—changed in a way that could not be undone. Her daughter, Lisa, had noticed. “Mom, you never come over for Sunday dinners anymore,” she had said last month, and Margaret had heard the hurt in her voice. She had not known how to explain that the walk from her car to Lisa’s front door, past the corner where two teenagers loitered in hoodies, had become an ordeal she could no longer face.

What finally brought Margaret to seek help was a morning in late February, when she found herself standing frozen in the hotel supply closet, her hand on a box of printer paper, unable to remember why she had come in. The panic had been rising for weeks, and she had realized, with a clarity that felt like a verdict, that she was running out of room to hide. She made the appointment because she was exhausted, and because she could no longer pretend that the woman she used to be was coming back. What she hoped for, in the quietest part of herself, was not to forget—she knew she would never forget—but to stop being afraid of her own life. What she feared most was that the damage was permanent, and that the person she had become was all that was left.
